tracks.about: the kernel: status values, write-once Parts, recorded calculations and all-or-nothing ticks

claims.claim: A Part made directly is a leaf of the lineage DAG: composition must be None.
None is a legitimate value (distinct from 'no Part'); the wrapper must not treat it as absent.
Mutating the original after wrapping must not change the Part (else lineage values drift).
Mutating a returned value must not change the Part (attack: mutation through a reference).
Deep copy must handle cycles and keep their shape (naive recursive copy would recurse forever).
If deepcopy fails the error must surface (not be swallowed into a half-built Part).
Calculations are behaviour, not data: a stateful callable object must keep its identity (copying it would orphan its state).
Parts are shared across lineage; any attribute assignment must raise AttributeError.
Two Parts with equal values are different lineage nodes; graphs (A5) rely on identity.
Addresses must be '<px|fn|sc>.<non-empty>'; every operation must reject anything else with ValueError.
A non-str address is a type error, not a value error.
Any non-empty remainder after a known namespace is legal (case-sensitive prefix).
A rejected set must have no side effects.
Parts are identities: set returns its argument and get returns that very object every time.
Only Parts may be bound; a raw value would have no lineage slot. The address must remain free.
Write-once: there is no replacement, even with the same Part or an equal value.
Callers can catch the whole family with PxCError.
Missing is distinguishable from None and can be caught as KeyError.
has must be a pure query.
The one enforced namespace rule: fn.* addresses hold callables. Rejection leaves the address free.
px.* and sc.* accept any value (including callables): only fn.* is policed.
entries() is a tuple of (address, Part) in binding order, unaffected by later bindings.
compose runs the calculation on named inputs and binds the result Part at `into`.
References may be string addresses or Part objects (unbound Parts included).
The calculation receives exactly one positional dict {name: value}, in the caller's input order.
Omitted, None, and empty inputs are equivalent: the calculation sees {}.
Attack: a calculation mutates its argument; the input Part must be untouched.
Attack: the calculation keeps a reference to what it returned and mutates it later.
Calculations are function-valued Parts, so a calculation may make one (needed for fn.* outputs).
The lineage DAG is made of the very Part objects used (A5 will traverse it).
Lineage must not be editable through the Composition.
Mutating the dict passed as `inputs` afterwards must not alter recorded lineage.
A diamond a -> (b, c) -> d: both branches must point at the SAME root Part, roots have no composition.
Preflight: occupancy is checked before the calculation runs, no receipt, original kept.
Check order is part of the contract: `into` is validated first.
The calculation must resolve to a function-valued Part; nothing runs, no receipt, `into` stays free.
Every input problem is found before the calculation runs; no receipt; `into` stays free.
An invalid target address is a preflight failure too.
A raising calculation: same exception object re-raised, address stays free, a retry can succeed.
A failed run is testimony too: status FAILED, into, composition, error, and no output.
Composing a non-callable into fn.* runs, then fails the namespace rule: TypeError, FAILED receipt, address free.
If wrapping the output fails (uncopyable value) the compose fails cleanly like any other failure.
While a compose into `into` is running, `into` is occupied: a calculation writing to it gets AddressOccupiedError.
A PRODUCED receipt points at the bound output and the very Composition on that output.
Receipts testify to compositions only; plain set is not a computation.
Receipts come back as a tuple in order of occurrence; they cannot be edited.
Normal exit binds everything, in compose order, with one PRODUCED receipt each tagged with the tick id.
Dependent steps (belief update) must read the previous step by address before commit; lineage points at the staged Part.
Isolation: store queries during an open tick show committed state only (no half-updated belief).
Only one tick at a time and no side-door writes: otherwise atomicity cannot be guaranteed.
Atomicity: if the block raises, NOTHING is bound; each compose gets a FAILED receipt carrying the escaping exception.
A calculation failure escaping the block: earlier composes carry that exception; the failed one keeps its own (same object).
If the block catches a compose failure and then raises a different exception, each receipt keeps the right error.
Rollback must release staged addresses and the tick lock so the work can be retried.
A compose failure the block handles does not roll back; its FAILED receipt sits in attempt order between PRODUCED ones.
Same preflight rules inside a tick: raise, no receipt; the tick can continue and commit.
Policing of fn.* output callability holds inside ticks too.
Degenerate tick: nothing staged, nothing recorded, store usable.
Using a scope after its block ended would bypass atomicity; every method must raise TickInProgressError.
A bad tick id is rejected on entry without leaving the store stuck in 'tick open'.
Receipts identify their tick; ungrouped composes have tick None.
For any JSON-like value: Part(v).value == v, and containers are never the same object (capture holds).
Model check: replaying random sets against a first-writer-wins dict must match the store exactly.
compose over N named inputs equals sum(); also checks inputs may be arbitrarily many.

sections.name: Clause 1: the five statuses exist and are distinct

claims.claim: The five epistemic states must be distinct members, or callers cannot tell 'unknown' from 'never measured'.

sections.name: Clause 2: KNOWN requires a value, others forbid it

claims.claim: A KNOWN judgment carries its value, which is the whole point of KNOWN.
Falsy values are legitimate knowledge (e.g. 'the pit is absent' = False); only None is forbidden.
KNOWN with value None is a contradiction in terms and must raise ValueError.
Only KNOWN may carry a value; otherwise a consumer might trust a value that is not established (even falsy ones).
UNKNOWN / NOT_OBSERVED / NOT_APPLICABLE need no value and may have an empty or a non-empty reason.

sections.name: Clause 3: INVALID needs a real reason

claims.claim: INVALID without an explanation is undebuggable; blank/whitespace reasons count as missing.
INVALID with a real reason is the one legal shape for INVALID.
Strings and ints must not masquerade as Status, or typos would silently create 'valid' judgments.
reason is human text; a non-str reason is a programming error (TypeError).
Judgments are shared between packages; mutation after the fact would change someone else's belief.
Equal judgments must be interchangeable as dict keys / set members.
KNOWN(False) must differ from UNKNOWN: 'known to be false' is not 'do not know'.

tracks.about: propositional logic: formulas, evaluation with unknowns, model enumeration, entailment, a proof checker, induction exercises

claims.claim: Sanity: enough cases, unique names, every case has the promised keys (a broken fixture must fail loudly).
Structure -> canonical string must equal the fixture string exactly (the cross-language format contract).
string -> structure via the test-suite's reference parser round-trips (checks grammar and fixture agree).
variables() and size() agree with the oracle.
Same rows, same values, same ORDER as the oracle.
Two-valued evaluate reproduces every oracle row.
models / is_satisfiable / is_valid agree with the oracle; models are exactly the True rows, in order.
The shared list of illegal names (JS port must reject the same ones).
Every premise and query string equals to_str of its structure.
The KB has 3 models: no pit at P11/P12/P21, breeze at B21 forces (P22 or P31). A3 weights these models.
KB |= query (or not) exactly as the oracle says, e.g. KB |= ~P12, KB |= ~P21, KB !|= P22, KB !|= ~P22.
countermodel returns the oracle's FIRST countermodel (or None when entailed).
The four facts the planner asked for, independent of the JSON: ~P12 yes, ~P21 yes, P22 no, ~P22 no.
Const holds exactly a bool.
Const(1) would make Const(1) == Const(True) by Python equality and corrupt hashing; only real bools allowed.
Names matching [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* are legal; 'True' (capitalised) and 'trueish' are not reserved.
Anything outside the ASCII identifier grammar, or the reserved atoms true/false, is a ValueError (else to_str would not round-trip).
A non-str name is a TypeError (distinct from a malformed str).
Every operand slot rejects non-Formula values with TypeError, so ill-formed trees cannot exist.
isinstance(x, Formula) must hold for every node class (used by checks elsewhere).
Frozen: shared sub-trees must never change under their users.
Two separately built, structurally identical formulas are interchangeable as dict keys.
No normalisation: And(a,b) != And(b,a), And != Or, grouping matters. (Semantic equivalence is is_valid(Iff(..)), not ==.)
Different node classes with 'similar' payloads must not collide: Const(True) vs Var('True') etc.
Copying must not break structural equality (guards against identity-based eq/hash).
For any f: a deep copy equals f and hashes the same; this is the hash/eq contract.
variables returns a frozenset of the names occurring anywhere, without duplicates.
Degenerate: no Var nodes -> empty frozenset (not None, not error).
Passing a str instead of a Formula is a bug in the caller: TypeError.
variables agrees with an independent naive traversal.
size is TREE size: shared sub-formulas are counted each time they occur.
Non-formulas are rejected with TypeError.
to_str must produce exactly the canonical string (A2's parser round-trips it): fully parenthesised, ASCII, single spaces.
Non-formulas are rejected with TypeError.
The grammar in the docstring is unambiguous: a strict reference parser recovers exactly f from to_str(f).
Shape check: parentheses balance and the only spaces are the single ones around binary operators.
Depth 200 under the default recursion limit must work (implementations: prefer an explicit stack).
Left- and right-leaning binary chains of depth 200 for every connective.
Structural equality and hashing of two separately-built depth-200 formulas must not overflow the stack.
A premise step needs no cites argument.
Malformed steps are TypeErrors at construction, so check() only sees well-typed data.
Reasons and serialisation use the snake_case rule names.
Degenerate: no steps -> nothing unjustified (also with no premises).
A premise may be restated, and premises may be listed in any order.
A separately built but equal formula counts as the premise; premises may come from a generator.
From p->q and p, conclude q; cites are (implication, antecedent).
From p->q and ~q, conclude ~p; cites are (implication, negated consequent).
and_intro builds And(f[i], f[j]) (i==j allowed); the eliminations pick the left/right conjunct.
or_intro_left/right allow ANY formula as the new disjunct (even an unrelated or constant one).
~~p |- p; and ~~~p |- ~p (strip exactly two negations).
A six-step derivation mixing rules (and_elim -> modus_ponens -> and_intro).
From p->q and q, concluding p is a fallacy; no cite order makes modus_ponens accept it.
From p->q and ~p, concluding ~q is a fallacy; modus_tollens must not accept it.
The contract is (implication first, antecedent second); (antecedent, implication) is rejected.
MP must produce exactly the consequent, from exactly the antecedent.
And(f[i], f[j]) is ordered: citing (p, q) cannot justify And(q, p).
and_elim_left/right are not interchangeable.
Eliminating from an Or (or a bare variable) is invalid.
or_intro_left needs Or(f[i], X); putting f[i] on the right is or_intro_right, and vice versa.
~p |- p is classical-looking nonsense: a single negation must be rejected.
MT with a cited step that is not ~q is rejected.
A 'premise' not in the premise list is smuggling in an assumption.
premise takes zero cites.
Step 2 may only cite indices 0 and 1: own, later, negative and out-of-range indices break the proof's acyclicity.
Step 0 citing step 1 which cites step 0: both are non-earlier cites, first bad step is 0.
Each rule has a fixed arity; the reason must mention 'cites'.
Steps 2 and 4 are both invalid; the checker must report 2 and stop.
Reason text starts with 'step <i> (<rule>): ' so tooling can parse it.
Results are values; mutation must fail.
Completeness+soundness of the oracle: any chain built from the documented rules is accepted by check, and every line is entailed.
Soundness of the CHECKER: corrupt one line of a valid proof; if it still checks ok, every line must still be entailed by the premises.
Each connective matches its classical truth table on all four inputs.
Results are real bools (``is True``), including for Const-only formulas needing no assignment.
x or not x is true under both assignments; x and not x under neither.
Missing variable -> UnassignedVariableError (a KeyError) carrying the name.
When several are missing the error names the alphabetically first one (deterministic message).
evaluate RAISES even when the missing variable cannot affect the result (that is what evaluate_partial is for).
Irrelevant assignment entries do not matter.
Assignment values must be real bools; 1/0 would silently work in Python and hide bugs.
Strong Kleene tables, hard-coded: e.g. F and U = F, T or U = T, F implies U = T, U iff anything = U.
Not flips known values and leaves unknown unknown.
The headline Kleene case: False and x is KNOWN False regardless of x, in either operand position.
False -> x and x -> True are KNOWN True; True -> x and x -> False stay UNKNOWN.
x or not x, x and not x, x->x, x<->x are UNKNOWN for unassigned x: Kleene logic does not realise both x's are the same.
KNOWN must propagate through deep structure: (x or y) and False = False; Not(F and x) = True.
UNKNOWN reason is exactly 'unassigned: ' + sorted names of ALL missing variables of f (even irrelevant ones).
KNOWN results carry no reason, even if some irrelevant variable was unassigned.
Degenerate input: nothing to assign, so always KNOWN.
With every variable assigned the answer is KNOWN and equals evaluate.
Extra keys are ignored; a non-bool value for a variable that occurs in f is a TypeError.
On a total assignment evaluate_partial is KNOWN and equals evaluate (the two evaluators must not disagree).
If evaluate_partial says KNOWN v, then EVERY completion of the partial assignment evaluates to v (Kleene soundness).
Assigning one more variable never changes a KNOWN answer (information only helps).
Enumeration order is itertools.product([F,T]) over sorted names: the contract that countermodel and A3 rely on.
Sorting is plain str order: 'B' < '_' < 'a'; each dict's keys are in that order.
Const(True) has exactly one model (the empty assignment); Const(False) has none.
x and not x: 0 models; x or not x: 2 models (over its one variable).
Extra names in `over` are free variables: each doubles the model count, and ordering uses the sorted union.
Duplicates in `over` do not multiply the models.
`over` must cover variables(f); otherwise the models would be ill-defined.
models returns a real iterator (iter(x) is x), so callers can stream/limit it.
Mutating one yielded dict must not affect the others (a reused dict object is a classic bug).
truth_table lists ALL rows (including False) in enumeration order.
Zero variables -> a single row with the empty assignment.
Rows must not share assignment dicts.
models/truth_table agree with a naive enumerator, including ORDER.
Tautology: valid+sat. Contradiction: unsat+not valid. Contingent: sat, not valid.
Degenerate: no variables, one (empty) assignment.
Peirce's law and De Morgan are valid; affirming the consequent as a formula is not.
is_valid(f) == not is_satisfiable(Not(f)): the duality that defines validity.
is_satisfiable / is_valid agree with a naive enumeration.
No premises: the conclusion must be a tautology.
Ex falso: inconsistent premises entail any conclusion, even one over a fresh variable.
{p->q, p} entails q; {p->q, q} does NOT entail p.
Variables only in the conclusion count: {a} does not entail b, but entails a or b.
premises may be any iterable (consumed once); a lone Formula instead of an iterable is a TypeError.
No countermodel exactly when the entailment holds.
The FIRST countermodel in the module order is returned (not any/last/random).
Keys: the union of all variables, even ones irrelevant to the failure.
Const(False) has the countermodel {} (the single empty assignment).
entails/countermodel agree with a naive search; countermodel is None iff entails; and it really is a countermodel.
200 negations: even count -> same value, odd -> flipped (both evaluators).
Depth-200 left/right chains: models, validity, satisfiability and Kleene shortcuts all work.
entails/countermodel on depth-200 formulas (single variable, so enumeration is tiny).
Structural equality/hash so mirror(mirror(t)) == t is meaningful.
Every Node has exactly two Tree children; a raw value is a TypeError.
Leaf stores anything (the proofs never inspect it).
Mirrors the two cases of the structural induction: leaf unchanged; node swaps and recurses.
A palindromic tree is a fixed point (rules out a mirror that returns a constant).
Guards against a do-nothing mirror.
Non-trees are a TypeError.
Depth 200 must not overflow the default recursion limit; double mirror restores it.
mirror(mirror(t)) == t for every tree. Sampling is evidence; PROOFS.md proves it by structural induction.
mirror keeps size and height and reverses the left-to-right leaf order.
A single Leaf: size 1, height 0.
Hand-computed values: size counts internal nodes too; height counts edges on the longest path.
Height is a max, not a sum or the left side only.
Depth-200 comb: 2n+1 nodes, height n.
Non-trees are a TypeError.
In a full binary tree nodes = 2*leaves - 1 and height < size; ties tree_size to an independent leaf count.
Base case n=0 is 0 (the empty sum); then 1, 3, 6, ...
SAMPLES n(n+1)/2 for n in 0..2000. This test does NOT prove the claim for all n -- tracks/A1/PROOFS.md does (by induction).
T(n) = T(n-1) + n: the inductive step, checked on samples (not a proof).
Big n stays an exact int (no float drift).
Only real ints (not bool, not float) are accepted: TypeError.
The sum 1..n is undefined for negative n: ValueError.
If triangular used n*(n+1)//2, comparing it with that formula would be circular. Source must loop/sum and avoid *, /, //.
Tree is an abstract sum type: only Leaf and Node are trees. A bare Tree() must be

tracks.about: the Calc language: a table-driven lexer, two formula parsers, a type checker, step-by-step and direct evaluators, and the bridge back to logic and the kernel

claims.claim: Each connective maps to one fixed Calc shape (implication is `not x or y`, iff is `==` on Bools), so other code can rely on the structure.
`Var("not")` is a legal logic variable but not a legal Calc one: from_formula raises ValueError instead of producing a broken term.
Strings, numbers and None are not Formulas: TypeError.
Calc nodes are not logic Formulas even though they look alike (Var, Not): TypeError.
The result typechecks as Bool whenever its variables are declared Bool, and its free variables are exactly the formula's.
For every formula: free_vars preserved and type Bool under an all-Bool environment.
Names ascending, smallest outermost, each bound to a BoolLit; the exact nesting is the cross-language encoding.
No names, no wrapping.
Like logic.evaluate: 1 and None are not truth values here (TypeError).
THE BRIDGE LAW: calc.evaluate(lets(a) around from_formula(f)) is logic.evaluate(f, a) for every formula and total assignment (a real bool, not 1/0).
The small-step trace of the bridged program ends in the same BoolLit as logic.evaluate: the three evaluators (logic, big-step, small-step) agree.
Parse each canonical fixture string (A2 parser), embed it (bridge), evaluate with Calc: every row equals the A1 fixture's independently computed truth table.

The Russell & Norvig corner KB has exactly 3 models in the A1 fixture; Calc, evaluating the conjunction of the premises on all 128 assignments, finds the same 3 (the A3 numbers 4/9, 4/9, 1/9 start here).
The same mistake has two faces: logic raises UnassignedVariableError, Calc reports the term as INVALID statically (unbound variable) and STUCK dynamically.
The bridge law needs a TOTAL assignment: `false and x` evaluates in Calc without x (short-circuit) but logic.evaluate rejects the missing variable.
The embedded program prints and re-parses to itself: parse_formula -> from_formula -> to_source -> parse_calc is the identity on the Calc side.
200 nested negations bridge without recursion errors: even depth gives the same value.
`(1+2)+(3+4)` has 3 steps, so 4 Parts at px.run.0..3 holding index/source/outcome records that match calc.trace.
Each step's composition has the single input `prev` = the Part of the previous step (identity), down to step 0 whose only input is `program`.
Steps >= 1 are produced by the same calculation Part (one rule applied repeatedly); every calculation Part holds a callable.
Feeding the calculations different inputs gives different, correct outputs: they parse their input and apply calc.step, they do not replay stored answers.
One tick: n+1 PRODUCED receipts, all with tick == prefix, in step order (that is dsdk.core tick semantics showing through).
A value has an empty step list: one Part, outcome 'value', returned and bound at px.<prefix>.0, with only the `program` input.
`(1+1)+true` steps once then is stuck: two Parts, the last has outcome 'stuck' (a stuck run is data too, not an error).
Only px.<prefix>.<i> addresses are bound; no fn.* or sc.* bookkeeping.
Different prefixes do not collide; each chain stays internally linked.
Write-once store: a second run with the same prefix raises AddressOccupiedError; the first trace is untouched.
If px.run.2 is already taken, steps 0 and 1 must NOT remain bound, and their receipts must be FAILED: the single tick rolled back.
Prefix validation happens first: no Parts, no receipts, no open tick left behind.
store must be a PxC and expr an Expr.
The bridge does not work around dsdk.core: with a tick already open, opening its own tick raises TickInProgressError.
A 100-step trace gives 101 Parts linked by identity; because records hold source STRINGS (not 100-deep ASTs) nothing blows up in the store's deep copies.
For ANY term (stuck or not): n+1 records equal [index, to_source, outcome] of calc.trace(e), and the lineage has n+1 Parts.
IntLit holds an exact Python int of any sign and size.
IntLit(True) would make IntLit(1) == IntLit(True) by Python equality; bool is rejected with TypeError.
BoolLit(1) is a TypeError: only True/False.
ASCII identifiers are fine; near-keywords (`letx`, `Not`, `android`, `iff`) are not keywords.
Anything outside [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* or equal to a Calc keyword is a ValueError (else to_source would not parse back).
A non-str name is a TypeError, distinct from a malformed str.
The seven operators + - * < == and or are the whole set.
OPS is the exact operator tuple in the documented order.
An operator outside OPS is a ValueError (None included: it is simply not one of them).
Every child slot is type-checked: strings, ints, None and even logic Formulas are TypeErrors.
`let if = 1 in 2` cannot be represented: keyword and malformed binder names are ValueError, non-str is TypeError.
Every concrete node class derives from Expr (parsers and checkers dispatch on that).
IntLit(1) != BoolLit(True); operand order matters; no normalisation (a+b != b+a, (a+b)+c != a+(b+c)).
Equal nodes hash equal; this is what lets traces and caches key on terms.
Assigning to a node raises FrozenInstanceError (immutable AST).
size is the tree size (every occurrence counts; the let binder is not a node).
Depth 200 works: right_sum(200) has 401 nodes.
A let binds its name only in the BODY: the bound expression sees the outer scope, so `let x = x in x` still has x free.
substitute replaces FREE occurrences only: the bound expression of a let is always searched, its body only if the binder differs from `name`.
Substituting an absent name is the identity (by equality); the input node is immutable anyway.
Only IntLit/BoolLit may be substituted (TypeError otherwise): a Var would be capturable under a binder, a literal never is.
Non-Expr term and non-str name are TypeErrors.
Depth 200 under the default recursion limit; every `x` leaf is replaced.
Exactly the two literal node types are values; a variable is not.
Values convert to Python int/bool and back, keeping bool and int apart (bool is checked first).
Floats, None and strings are not Calc values.
A non-value Expr is a ValueError and a non-Expr is a TypeError.
Passing a non-Expr (including a logic Formula) is a TypeError, not an AttributeError or a silent answer.
to_source prints with single spaces and parentheses around every compound node; the exact text is the cross-language format.
Depth 200 prints without recursion errors and agrees with the test-suite's own printer.
evaluate returns an int for Int results and a real bool for Bool results (True != the int 1 here).
Evaluation that cannot continue raises StuckError (not TypeError/KeyError/NameError); `.term` is the evaluated program.
No overflow or float rounding: 30-digit operands multiply exactly, and 2**200 by repeated products stays exact.
`1 == true` is stuck although Python says 1 == True; `evaluate` of an Int literal is never a bool and vice versa.
evaluate is the oracle the small-step functions are compared with, so it must not be implemented via step or trace.
`let y = x in ...` inside a scope that rebinds x later still sees the OUTER x's value: the binding is evaluated where it is written.
A 200-deep right-nested sum evaluates to 201 and a 200-deep chain of lets to its innermost binding.
Only an Expr is evaluated; a str is not parsed implicitly.
Precedence (or < and < not < comparison < + - < *) and left-associativity decide the tree; compared with an independently read canonical form.
`not true and false` is (not true) and false = false, while not (true and false) = true: a precedence slip changes the answer.
`1 < 2 < 3` and `1 == 2 == 3` and `1 < 2 == true` are rejected (compare results are not chained).
`-3` after an operator is a literal, after an operand it is subtraction: `1 -2` is 1 - 2, `1 - -2` has a negative literal.
Integer literals are parsed with int(): no float rounding for 30 digits.
Each ParseError points at the start of the first offending token (or the end of input) and its expected-set contains the kinds the grammar requires there.
`-x` and `--2` fail at the token after the sign, and the only acceptable thing there is INT.
Illegal characters are LexErrors (a LangError, not a ParseError) with the index of the character.
`1 2 @` has a parse error at 2 and a lex error at 4: the whole text is tokenized first so the LexError wins.
Only str is parsed.
to_source prints a negative literal as `-n`, and parse_calc reads it back to the same node.
parse_calc(to_source(e)) == e for EVERY Expr (well-typed or not): printing loses nothing.
to_source(parse_calc(s)) == s for canonical s, and the independent printer agrees with to_source.
200 levels of parentheses, `not`, let-bodies, else-branches and a 200-term left chain parse under the default recursion limit.
PROGRESS: a closed well-typed term is a value or can step. (Stuck = a bug in either the typing rules or the step rules.)
PRESERVATION: if e : T and e -> e' then e' : T (the generator gives e : T; every term of the trace must keep T).
TYPE SAFETY: a well-typed closed program evaluates to a value whose Python type matches its static type.
evaluate(e) == the value at the end of trace(e), with the same Python type (two independent implementations agree).
Even for ill-typed and open terms: trace ends in a value  <=>  evaluate returns it; trace ends stuck  <=>  evaluate raises StuckError.
The test-suite's own environment-passing evaluator (no substitution) gives the same answer as evaluate on ANY term: substitution and environments are two views of one semantics.
TERMINATION MEASURE: size strictly decreases at each step, so trace length <= size(e) - 1 and evaluation always halts (see tracks/A2/PROOFS.md).
free_vars(e') is a subset of free_vars(e) for every step e -> e' (substitution only removes variables).
CONTRAPOSITIVE OF SAFETY: if a closed term's trace ends stuck, typecheck must have reported INVALID.
Under env {x: Int, y: Bool}, a KNOWN result means every free variable is in the environment; an unbound-variable error names a free variable.
If x:Int |- e : T and v : Int then e[x := v] : T in the empty environment. This is the lemma that makes the `let` case of preservation work.
Same lemma with a Bool variable and Bool literal.
The generator's closed terms are closed: free_vars is empty, so evaluate never reports an unbound variable for them.
step applies exactly one rule (call-by-value, left to right, leftmost-innermost, and/or short-circuit) or returns None.
A value does not step to itself (that would loop traces forever): the result is None.
VALUE (a literal), STEP (a rule applies), STUCK (neither): a stuck term is not a value and not a term that can still reduce.
classify is derived from step: literals are VALUE, other terms that step are STEP, all remaining terms are STUCK.
`(if true then 1 else (1 + true))` is ill-typed statically but reduces to the value 1 (not stuck); `(1 + true)` is stuck.
trace returns [e0, ..., en] including the start and the final value/stuck term, each obtained by one step.
In `(1+1) + (2+2)` the FIRST step must reduce the left addition; a right-first implementation gives `(1 + 1) + 4`.
With a stuck left operand the right operand is NEVER reduced (trace length 1); left-to-right evaluation is observable here.
`let x = (1 + true) in 5` is stuck under call-by-value; a lazy (call-by-name) reading would reach 5.
Neither branch is touched until the condition is a value, and the untaken one is dropped without a single step on it.
`false and <stuck>` finishes with false; `<stuck> and false` is stuck: the order of operands is semantics.
Substitution during `let` must skip rebound names and never alter the bound expression of an inner let that mentions the outer name.

right_sum(200) has 200 additions: 201 terms, the last is the integer 201, and nothing recurses past the limit.
Only Exprs are accepted; strings are not parsed implicitly.
`Let(x, v, body)` with v a value rewrites straight to body[x:=v]; no intermediate Let remains.
A well-typed closed program is Judgment(KNOWN, Type) with empty reason; shadowing may change a variable's type inside its scope only.

None means empty, and a read-only mapping works.

sections.name: strict mode rejects everything else, with exact errors

claims.claim: Anything but the exact canonical grammar is a ParseError at the first offending token (or end of input), carrying what was expected there.
parse_formula(text) is strict; only relaxed=True accepts `a & b`.
Relaxed mode applies ~ > & > | > -> > <->, with -> right-associative and & | <-> left-associative; the result printed canonically pins the tree.
`a -> b -> c` is a -> (b -> c): the other grouping is a DIFFERENT formula (they disagree at a=F,b=F,c=F), so the choice is not cosmetic.
For & | <-> left vs right grouping gives equal truth tables (they are associative), so choosing left-associativity cannot change meaning.
`~a & b` is (~a) & b, never ~(a & b); the two differ at a=T,b=F.
Relaxed is a superset of strict: for canonical text both modes give the same Formula.
Relaxed ParseErrors point at the first offending token (or the end) and list the token kinds the grammar would accept there; 'END' marks 'end of input allowed'.
Illegal characters (including Unicode look-alikes) raise LexError with their index in both modes; LexError is a LangError but not a ParseError.
`a a @` has a parse error at 2 and a lex error at 4; the whole text is tokenized first, so the LexError wins.
parse_formula only takes str.
A grammar with no precedence gives `a | b & c` two trees, in the documented order (root `|` first).
The two readings of `a | b & c` disagree on a model (a=T,b=F,c=F), so a parser must pick one: precedence is what picks it.
Precedence resolves the ambiguity: `&` binds tighter, so relaxed gives the FIRST tree (a | (b & c)).
Root operator index goes left to right; for each root, left trees vary slowest then right trees.
With k operators and no precedence there are Catalan(k) distinct trees (1,1,2,5,14,42): the combinatorial cost of ambiguity.
The precedence-free grammar has no ~ and no parentheses; other shapes are ParseErrors.
Illegal characters are LexErrors here too.
For `atom op atom op ...` the relaxed parser returns exactly one of the Catalan(k) readings: precedence selects, never invents.
parse_formula(to_str(f)) == f for every Formula: nothing is lost or reassociated by printing and reading.
to_str(parse_formula(s)) == s for canonical s (the other half of the round trip).
Relaxed mode is a conservative extension of strict mode.
An independent minimal-parenthesis printer (using the documented precedences) plus arbitrary whitespace parses back to the same tree in relaxed mode.
Minimal-parenthesis text that differs from to_str(f) must be rejected by strict mode (only canonical text is accepted).
Parsing the canonical text of f and evaluating agrees with evaluating f itself on all-true and all-false assignments (smoke link to dsdk.logic).
200 levels of ~, parentheses, left chains and right chains parse in both modes under the default recursion limit.
Relaxed input -> logic.to_str of the parsed formula equals the fixture's canonical string, and that string is a fixed point of strict parsing.
Each invalid relaxed string fails with the fixture's error kind, offset and expected-set.
Each invalid strict string fails with the fixture's error kind, offset and expected-set.
At least 6 valid and 6 invalid programs, unique names, every AST decodes through the node constructors (and re-encodes to itself).
parse_calc(source) is the fixture AST (compared structurally and as encoded JSON) and prints back to the fixture canonical text.
typecheck gives KNOWN with the fixture type, or INVALID with exactly the fixture reason (tag and offending node).
The full small-step trace (every intermediate term), its length and the final outcome equal the fixture.
evaluate returns the fixture value (decimal text compared, so 30-digit results are exact) and its Python type, or raises StuckError exactly for stuck programs.
Type safety on the fixture: a `valid` program (typechecks) ends its trace in a value of the static type.
Some ill-typed fixture programs (`false and (1 + true)`) still evaluate to a value: the static check is conservative, so INVALID and STUCK are different facts.
The invalid list must contain stuck programs AND ill-typed programs that run, otherwise the lesson is missing (names are the contract).
Lex/parse errors carry the fixture offset; parse errors' expected-sets include the fixture's required kinds.
Each token kind in the module table lexes from its canonical text as ONE token covering the whole input.
start/end index the source string so that text == source[start:end]; later passes report errors with these offsets.
The longest accepting prefix wins, and a failed longer attempt (`<-` not followed by `>`) falls back: `<->` is one IFF, `<-b` is LT MINUS NAME.
`<->` is the single kind IFF while `<-b` is LT, MINUS, NAME: the ambiguity a regex-free DFA must resolve by backtracking.
After `<->` or `->` is consumed a stray `>` is an illegal start: the error offset is that character, not the start of the operator.
`true` is TRUE but `trueish`, `true1`, `True` and `_true` are NAMEs: keywords are looked up after the DFA reads the whole identifier.
The keyword kind is text.upper() and Token.text keeps the source spelling.
The default keyword set is empty, so `let`, `true`, `in` are NAMEs (formulas allow variables called `if`).
CALC_KEYWORDS is exactly the ten reserved words of Calc (the parser and Var validation rely on it).
Whitespace separates tokens but is not emitted unless asked for.
With keep_whitespace a run of spaces/tabs/newlines is ONE WS token (so the strict parser can see `a  &` has two spaces).
Empty input is no tokens; blank input is no tokens (or one WS token when kept). Parsers rely on this to report 'unexpected end'.
Unicode look-alikes (Arabic-Indic digits, fullwidth letters, NBSP, arrows, emoji) are NOT letters/digits/spaces here: LexError with the code-point index of the FIRST bad character.
Only str is tokenizable; bytes must not be silently accepted.
char_class must not use str.isalpha/isdigit/isspace (they accept é, ٣ and NBSP); it is a fixed ASCII classification.
CHAR_CLASS_NAMES is the closed set of class names char_class can return.
A str of length != 1 is a ValueError.
A non-str is a TypeError.

sections.name: the DFA table is inspectable data

claims.claim: The transition table and accepting map are plain data that equal the module docstring entry by entry (a JS port can copy them).
Sanity of the machine: start is not accepting, all targets are real states, every state is reachable, class names are known, and no state except `start` and `lt_minus` is non-accepting.
Mutating a returned table (if it even allows it) must not change what the next default_dfa() returns.
`<-` ends in a NON-accepting state (so the lexer must backtrack), `<->` in the IFF state, `<-x` in no state.
The table is the single source of truth: delete `->` from it and `->` stops lexing; add letter-after-minus and `a-b` becomes one NAME.
100000 characters of one identifier, and 50000 tokens, lex fine (iteration, not recursion; linear time).

With whitespace kept the tokens tile the input (contiguous, texts concatenate to the input), each token re-lexes to itself, and no two ADJACENT tokens could have been one longer token (maximal munch).

tracks.about: graphs: BFS with witness paths, cycles, topological order, components, evidence-aware reachability, and graphs built from lineage, formulas and dsdk's own imports

claims.claim: A Part with no composition has no history: one node, no edges.

Strings and Parts are not formulas.

Property: node count == logic.size(f); n-1 edges; unique parent per non-root; all reachable from 0;

ast.walk semantics: nested imports count; text that merely looks like an import does not.

The argument may be a str; a directory that does not exist is FileNotFoundError.

The reason this graph exists: two packages importing each other is a cycle with a topological-sort failure.
Isolated nodes and flags survive; UNKNOWN and NOT_OBSERVED edges are dropped.
A path of KNOWN edges proves reachability: KNOWN True, and the reason shows the witness.
The empty path always exists, with no edges at all (and the reason has a single node).
The curriculum lesson: an inferred edge on the only route means 'maybe', never 'no' and never 'yes'.
The reason names each uncertain edge on the best candidate path, in walking order, with its evidence.
A known detour proves reachability even if a shorter uncertain edge exists: KNOWN True via the known path.
Both routes have exactly one uncertain edge, so the shorter route a->z is the best candidate.
2 hops with 2 uncertain edges loses to 3 hops with 1 uncertain edge: uncertainty is compared first.
No path even counting uncertain edges, but the world is open: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Only a closed world may conclude impossibility.
Closing the world does not turn an uncertain edge into a known one: KNOWN False needs NO path at all.
KNOWN False carries the value False (a legitimate known value), distinguishing it from UNKNOWN's None.
a->b known does not give b->a: directed graph, reverse query is open-world unknown (or closed-world False).
The reason shows the direction the path walks the edge, not the storage orientation.
Asking about a node the graph lacks is an ill-posed question: INVALID with the node named.
A known self-loop at a does not connect a to b.
No recursion limit and no quadratic blow-up on long chains, for both the known and the candidate search.
Equal uncertainty and hops: the path with the smaller index sequence wins (b before c).
s == t is (s,); disconnected is None; missing nodes raise MissingNodeError.
Property: the verdict equals the decision table computed from Floyd-Warshall on (known edges) / (all edges).
Property: candidate_path is a real path, and no path has fewer uncertain edges (or, equal, fewer hops).
The fixture set must contain every required shape, and building each case must succeed (broken fixtures fail loudly).
Adjacency lists and the adjacency matrix equal the fixture (node-ordered neighbours, 0/1 matrix).
BFS distances, parent pointers and discovery order from every node match the independent oracle.
The exact witness (tie-break included) for all ordered pairs; None where unreachable.
Whole-graph and rooted DFS pre/post orders follow the recursive definition.
find_cycle returns the first back edge in DFS order, or None; the verdict flag agrees.
Kahn's order (smallest index first), a CycleError with the witness, or GraphError for undirected graphs.
Weak components and SCCs in canonical form.
The 'missing reference' of the curriculum graph: E->Z with Z undeclared must raise, and name Z.
Every (source, target) Judgment -- status, value and exact reason -- including a missing source node.
Without `nodes=`, order is source-then-target per edge as listed; it fixes every later tie-break.

Edge objects, (u, v) and (u, v, w) tuples build equal graphs when they describe the same edges.

Graphs are frozen so they can be shared and hashed safely.
directed defaults to True and closed_world to False (the open-world default is deliberate).

In an undirected graph (a, b) and (b, a) are the same edge, stored once.
A KNOWN observation must not be weakened by an extra uncertain claim, in either listing order.

A self-loop is a real edge: it must survive construction and show in neighbours and the matrix diagonal.

bool is not a weight (True == 1 would hide bugs); strings and lists are not numbers.

Direction shows up as asymmetry; an undirected edge fills both cells.

index_of / neighbors / predecessors treat an absent node as a contract violation.

Without direction there is nothing to flip.

A partial mapping is MissingNodeError; two nodes mapped to one name is GraphError (no silent merge).
Plain {'source', 'target'} rows work with no options; unrelated keys are ignored.
source=/target= name the columns, so tables with 'src'/'dst' headers load without renaming.
weight/evidence/label columns are read when named; evidence accepts Status members and their string values.

A row without a source or target cannot be an edge: GraphError, not KeyError and not a skipped row.
If you name a weight column, every row must have it.
Duplicate rows merge exactly like duplicate edges; `nodes=` adds nodes that appear in no row.
The missing-reference rule holds for records too.
The adjacency matrix and the adjacency lists describe the same relation (both views are derived from it).
Shuffling and duplicating the input edges (with fixed nodes) yields an EQUAL graph.
For directed graphs reverse() exchanges successor and predecessor lists.
a->b->c joins into the single pair (a, c); an edge alone joins into nothing.
Output order is defined: r1 in input order, r2 in input order.

source=/target= select the columns, as in Graph.from_records.

Two different middle nodes give an entry of 2 (this is a count of middles, not of rows).
Undirected a-b: a-b-a is a 2-walk, so (a, a) and (b, b) are 2-hop pairs; the matrix diagonal is the degree.

Property (the point of this module): SELECT DISTINCT self-join == adjacency composition, duplicates or not.

Every package on disk is registered in tracks.toml and vice versa (same check as test_reuse, via the graph).
